summary: Bass Harbor Head Light, lit 1 September 1858 at the southwest tip of Mount Desert Island: a one-keeper station, automated in 1974, now managed by Acadia National Park.

lens.where: lantern on the tower; acrylic red shroud removed after 2020, red LED lamp

structures.note: Brick tower, 26 ft to the original focal plane (NRHP); about 32 ft in total (LighthouseFriends); NPS gives 37 ft including the lightning rod. The record's 1905 date belongs to the barn.
One and a half story, joined to the tower by a covered walk; raised ten inches in 1878; ell lengthened ten feet in 1900 (NRHP, Board 1900).
Bell house per NRHP (brick, erected 1876). LighthouseFriends describes a pyramidal bell tower of 1876. NPS dates its Bell House to 1897.
Brick fog-signal building; the Board's 1896-1897 report records a brick fog-signal house built. New England Lighthouses dates the new bell and building to 1898.
Brick oil house, 205 feet northwest of the tower (NEL).

access.note: Grounds, viewing areas and parking are open; the lighthouse interior is not open to the public. Acadia National Park manages the grounds.

facts.agency: National Park Service (Acadia National Park); U.S. Coast Guard keeps the right-of-way for the automated light

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record lists the brick tower as built 1905. The NRHP nomination and LighthouseFriends both date the tower to 1858; 1905 is the barn's date in the NRHP nomination.
The record gives the fog signal as 1876. The 1876 structure was a bell tower or bell house; the brick fog-signal building went up in 1897 (LighthouseFriends; Board 1896-1897 report).
The record names the U.S. Coast Guard. The National Park Service accepted the station on 8 July 2020; the Coast Guard keeps the right-of-way for the automated light.

notes_for_editor: Newspaper search (Chronicling America, via newspapers.py) for Bass Harbor Head was attempted twice and failed with HTTP 520 from loc.gov; no newspaper was read for this story. Sources 1 and 12 are all-rights-reserved community sites: facts restated in our words, with one short quotation from each. The USCG Historian's Bass Harbor page could not be read (archive copies returned only a frame). The 1855 appropriation date differs: LighthouseFriends gives an 18 August 1856 allocation after Franklin's 1855 report; NEL says soon after. The lens date is 1901 (NEL, NPS) or 1902 (LighthouseFriends). The bell-house date is 1876 (NRHP, LighthouseFriends) or 1897 (NPS). The fog-signal building date is 1897 (LighthouseFriends, Board) or 1898 (NEL). The transfer year is 2020 (NPS, LighthouseFriends) or 2018 (NEL). The 1938 fog figures (399 and 302) were matched to Bass Harbor Head by column position in the OCR (a row reading 'Bass Harbor Head, Maine 399 302') and were checked on the page image (Bulletin PDF page 31, printed p.127), where the row sits in the Total hours and Longest continuous run columns. The Board entries were checked in the corpus text: 1892 (scan p.374), 1894 (p.346), 1895 (p.224) and 1900 (p.47) with their page numbers confirmed by the page index. The 1896-1897 and 1901 entries were confirmed by their text only (the page index does not cover those OCR volumes), so the scan page 292 given in footnotes 8 and 10 is unconfirmed: open the URL before relying on the page number. The NPS gives a 52-acre 1937 purchase while the NRHP gives 2.5 acres for the station; the story uses neither. Dolliver's stint end conflicts (1921 vs 1912). The roster role heading 'Principal Lighthouse Keeper' is normalised to keeper, since this was a one-keeper station. Carroll Alley and Gerry Moores appear only in NEL's keeper list. Keeper Robert L. Archilles's spelling follows USLHS. Several keepers and families postdate 1960 and are named only in their public roles from the sources; the tenant household in the converted keeper's house is not named. The LighthouseFriends room count (five) conflicts with NEL's (four rooms and an attached kitchen); not used in the story. The NRHP OCR is imperfect; the quotations were checked against the cached text.

corrections.why: The NRHP nomination and LighthouseFriends date the brick tower to 1858. The 1905 date belongs to the barn (NRHP).
1876 was the bell tower or bell house. The brick fog-signal building was built in 1897 (LighthouseFriends; Board 1896-1897 report).
The National Park Service formally accepted the station from the Coast Guard on 8 July 2020; the Coast Guard retains the right-of-way for the automated light.
